newsitem.title: afghanistan: New Afghan rulers chase foes after taking Kabul.
newsitem.headline: New Afghan rulers chase foes after taking Kabul.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban militia pursued the forces of ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani into the north on Friday after capturing the capital Kabul and proclaiming strict Islamic rule.
Rabbani urged Afghans and faction leaders to resist the Taleban, saying their victory was fraught with danger.

Taleban sources, quoted by an Afghan news service in neighbouring Pakistan, said the Islamic militia fighters had chased the fleeing forces of Rabbani north of Kabul and were fighting at Charikar, capital of Parwan province.
There were no immediate details of the fighting, but the Taleban appeared to be taking aim at the Jabal-us-Seraj base of Rabbani's top military commander Ahmad Shah Masood.

The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) quoted a statement issued by Rabbani from an undisclosed place as appealing to people and faction leaders to resist Taleban, which earlier appealed for international recognition of its government.

Two years after their formation, the one-time band of Islamic student vigilantes took over a ruined capital, hanged former president Najibullah and his brother and proclaimed the complete enforcement of Islam in the war-wracked country.
In some of the first measures enforced, the Taleban barred women from offices until further orders and asked them to wear the traditional Islamic "hejab" veil when outside their homes.
Religious scholar Mullah Agha Gulabi said on official Kabul Radio that adulterers and drinkers must be killed.
"God says that those committing adultery should be stoned to death," he said.

"Anybody who drinks and says that it is not against the Koran, you have to kill him and hang his body for three days until people say this is the body of the drinker who did not obey the Koran and Allah's order," he said.

"We call upon the international community to recognise us as the government of the Islamic state of Afghanistan," Taleban spokesman Wakil Ahmad told Reuters by telephone from the southern Afghan town of Kandahar.
Neighbouring Pakistan appeared to signal the first recognition of the new regime by announcing it would dispatch officials for talks in Kabul.
Life appeared normal in the shattered capital, which government forces abandoned hours before the Taleban entered around 1.00 a.m. on Friday (2130 GMT Thursday).
The bodies of Najibullah, who led a Soviet-backed government until he was ejected in April 1992, and his brother Shahpur Ahmadzai were strung up in the centre of the city, watched by curious crowds.
The Taleban described ousted Rabbani, Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar and Masood as "national criminals" for not accepting a Taleban amnesty in return for a surrender.
The men fled Kabul before the Taleban marched in.
"We call upon the international community to recognise us as the government of the Islamic state of Afghanistan," Taleban spokesman Wakil Ahmad said.

Witnesses said Kabul's streets were bustling with pedestrians, cyclists and cars and shops and markets were open despite an Islamic holiday. Militia tanks had pulled back to sidestreets although fighters were still visible at key points.
People laden with belongings were seen returning to their homes in the eastern suburbs after fleeing earlier fighting.
All key government installations appeared to be in Taleban hands, including the Presidential Palace and the Ministries of Defence, Security and Foreign Affairs.

The country's currency, the afghani, surged to 11,000 to the U.S. dollar from the 18,500 level it was trading at before Kabul fell. "We think the afghani will strengthen when the market reopens tomorrow," money changer Javaid told Reuters.

Elsewhere, India stepped up security at the homes of former Afghan leaders living in New Delhi, police said. Paramilitary troops surrounded the house of Najibullah's widow and raised security near the house of former president Babrak Karmal.
The International Committee of the Red Cross said in Geneva the Taleban had agreed it could continue humanitarian relief operations, including approval for a 35-truck relief convoy.

In Tehran, Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani called on the Afghan factions to stop fighting and set up a joint administration. France also called for reconcilliation in Afghanistan and said Najibullah's execution was "regrettable."
The Taleban announced just hours after the takeover that an interim six-man ruling council would run the country.
A declaration by Taleban's supreme leader Mullah Mohammad Omar quoted by AIP, named his deputy, Mullah Mohammad Rabbani, no relation of the ousted president, to head the council.
Omar earlier proclaimed Afghanistan a "completely Islamic state" where a complete Islamic system would be enforced.
A Taleban commander named Musa said an amnesty had been declared for all government soldiers and officers who gave up.
"Taleban will not take revenge. We have no personal rancour. If the people find someone responsible for crimes in the past we will judge him according to Islamic law," he said.
